extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, journalists, and policymakers interested in disinformation and media manipulation
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of disinformation: its definitions, distinctions from related terms, frameworks for analysing campaigns (actors, techniques, content, distribution/effect), common tactics and modalities, ethical considerations, and research challenges and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: false or misleading information deliberately spread to deceive people, or to secure economic or political gain and which may cause public harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes disinformation as deliberate (intentional) and harmful; differentiates it from innocent inaccuracy. The lead paragraph also frames it as a public-harm risk and grounds subsequent discussion about actors, tactics, and impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation as orchestrated adversarial activity
rubrics_metrics.description: An orchestrated adversarial activity in which actors employ strategic deceptions and media manipulation tactics to advance political, military, or commercial goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises coordination and adversarial intent; highlights that campaigns weaponize rhetorical strategies and multiple forms of knowing (not only falsehoods but also truths, half-truths, and value judgments) to exploit identity-driven controversies and culture wars.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMMI taxonomy: disinformation, misinformation, malinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Disinformation: strategic dissemination of false information with the intention to cause public harm; (2) Misinformation: unintentional spread of false information; (3) Malinformation: factual information disseminated with the intention to cause harm. Abbreviated 'DMMI'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly consensus used to distinguish types of information disorder; useful for classification, policy responses, and research design because responses differ depending on intent and factuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABC framework — Manipulative Actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors who 'engage knowingly and with clear intent in viral deception campaigns' that are covert and designed to obfuscate the actor's identity and intent (examples: personas such as Guccifer 2.0, internet trolls, state media, military operatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of Camille François's ABC framework; identifies the responsible parties and their modalities (covert, persona-based, institutional). Use to attribute campaigns and design countermeasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABC framework — Deceptive Behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety of techniques viral deception actors use to enhance and exaggerate reach, virality and impact (examples: troll farms, internet bots, astroturfing, paid engagement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on tactics and technological/organisational behaviours that boost distribution; helpful for detection (patterns of amplification) and for platform interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABC framework — Harmful Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that causes harm including health misinformation, manipulated media such as deepfakes, online harassment, violent extremism, hate speech or terrorism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifies the substantive harms targeted by campaigns; informs severity assessments and prioritisation of mitigation (e.g., health vs. political misinformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution (Brookings addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical protocols that enable, constrain, and shape user behavior in a virtual space (i.e., how content is distributed and amplified by platform architecture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brookings recommends adding 'Distribution' to ABC to emphasise platform-level mechanisms (algorithms, recommendation systems, APIs) as central to impact and mitigation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree and Effect (Carnegie additions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree: the distribution of the content and the audiences it reaches; Effect: how much of a threat a given case poses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed metrics to supplement actor/behaviour/content analysis by quantifying reach and impact; useful for triage and risk assessment of disinformation incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeding and echoing stages of spread
rubrics_metrics.description: Two broad stages of disinformation spread on social media: 'seeding' (malicious actors strategically insert deceptions into an ecosystem) and 'echoing' (audiences disseminate disinformation as their own opinions, often incorporating it into confrontational narratives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework for analysing lifecycle and intervention points: block or disrupt seeding; counteract echoing via media literacy, fact-checking, and narrative interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of seeding (four main methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies show four main methods of seeding disinformation online: selective censorship; manipulation of search rankings; hacking and releasing (leaks); directly sharing disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies concrete insertion tactics platforms and defenders should monitor; each method implies different detection and remediation strategies (e.g., for search-rank manipulation vs hacked-doc dissemination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet manipulation / computational propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of online digital technologies, including algorithms, social bots, and automated scripts, for commercial, social, military, or political purposes — when used for political ends this is often called computational propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights technological enablers (bots, automation, algorithmic amplification) and links them to political objectives; suggests focusing on both technical signals and human networks for detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploiting online advertising and programmatic ad tech
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinformation is amplified through malpractice in online advertising (including machine-to-machine interactions of real-time bidding systems); programmatic advertising, lax oversight, monetization incentives, and dark money can be used to amplify disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points to economic incentives and ad-technology vulnerabilities as amplification vectors; suggests regulation/oversight of ad markets and transparency of political spending as mitigation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astroturfing
rubrics_metrics.description: A centrally coordinated campaign that mimics grassroots activism by making participants pretend to be ordinary citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise as a form of manufactured consensus; detection looks for coordination patterns, unnatural timing, or high similarity across supposedly independent accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake news (glossary entry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre: The deliberate creation of pseudo-journalism. Also: the term's instrumentalisation to delegitimise news media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between the genre of fabricated pseudo-journalism and the political label 'fake news' used to dismiss coverage; detection emphasises source provenance and journalistic indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspiracy theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuttals of official accounts that propose alternative explanations in which individuals or groups act in secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often persistent and identity-entangled; countering requires understanding underlying narratives and social drivers rather than just factual correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clickbait
rubrics_metrics.description: The deliberate use of misleading headlines and thumbnails to increase online traffic for profit or popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common amplification mechanism; combating it can involve platform policy on misleading metadata, publisher reputation signals, and consumer awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized mass communication, on a hidden agenda, with a mission to conform belief and action by circumventing individual reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links disinformation to longer-standing practices of mass persuasion; analysing intent, messaging frames, and channels helps differentiate propaganda from other forms of political communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudoscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts that claim the explanatory power of science, borrow its language and legitimacy but diverge substantially from its quality criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently used in health and environment-related disinformation; counterstrategies include promoting scientific literacy and transparency from legitimate scientific institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Echo chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: An epistemic environment in which participants encounter beliefs and opinions that coincide with their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes social/algorithmic clustering that amplifies reinforcement and reduces exposure to corrective information; measurement involves network analysis and content diversity metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trolling / coordinated 'click armies'
rubrics_metrics.description: Networked groups of digital influencers that operate 'click armies' designed to mobilize public sentiment — abusive or agitational behaviour coordinated to amplify messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifest in coordinated harassment, trending manipulation, or mass engagement campaigns; detection focuses on coordination, timing, and repeated patterns across networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hoax and forged materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Hoax: news in which false facts are presented as legitimate. Disinformation may also use forged documents, manuscripts, and photographs to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forensic analysis (metadata, provenance, corroboration) and rapid fact-checking are key countermeasures; forgers can cause legal and reputational blowback for perpetrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doxxing
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of online harassment that breaches privacy boundaries by releasing information intending physical and online harm to a target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classified as a harmful tactic often used in conjunction with disinformation campaigns to intimidate or silence critics; responses include platform takedowns, legal remedies, and protection for targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical test for disinformation in warfare
rubrics_metrics.description: An ethical test considers whether the disinformation was performed out of a motivation of good faith and acceptable according to the rules of war; some deceptions (e.g., inflatable tanks to mislead about force size) may be permissible, while disguising military targets as medical facilities is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a normative criterion for when information deception in conflict might be morally/legally acceptable; use case analysis against rules of armed conflict and proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and measurement challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinformation is intentionally written to mislead readers, producing data that is big, incomplete, unstructured, and noisy; detection algorithms derived from traditional news media are often ineffective; platforms sometimes discourage outside research access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights methodological limits for scholars (access to platform data, noisy signals). Recommends multidisciplinary methods, better platform transparency, and novel analytical approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical indicators of impact and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed empirical patterns include rapid online spread (often outpacing accurate information), concentration of exposure among small user groups, higher sharing of partisan-favouring false stories, and mixed evidence on measurable effects (e.g., on voting behaviour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple indicators — reach, engagement, audience composition, and experimental evidence — to assess real-world effects; beware that mass circulation does not automatically imply large behavioural effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended shifts in study and policy (alternative perspectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed moves: go beyond fact-checking and media literacy alone; go beyond technical/AI-only solutions; develop global (non-Americentric) perspectives; adopt market-oriented research on financial incentives and ad ecosystems; use multi-disciplinary approaches; study gendered disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and research prescriptions emphasise systemic, cultural, and economic analyses rather than narrowly technological fixes; suggests broader institutional and regulatory reforms.
